metaTitle: Mice Removal: Walls, Attics, Cars and Cleanup
metaDescription: Mice removal means sealing every 1/4-inch hole, snap-trapping until a week passes with no catches, and cleaning droppings wet. Steps for every space.
h1: Mice Removal: How to Get Mice Out and Clean Up After Them Safely
dek: How to get mice out of walls, attics, crawl spaces, garages and vehicles, find a dead mouse and deal with the smell, clean up droppings the way the CDC describes, and decide whether to hire the job out.
excerpt: Mice removal is three jobs: seal the holes, trap with snap traps until a week is clear, and disinfect droppings wet. Steps for walls, attics, crawl spaces, garages and cars.

quickAnswer.lead: **Mice removal is three jobs in order: seal every opening 1/4 inch or larger, trap the mice already inside with snap traps, and clean up droppings and nests wet, never with a broom or vacuum.** The [CDC's trapping instructions](https://www.cdc.gov/healthy-pets/rodent-control/trap-up.html) treat the rodents as gone when none is captured for a week and no new signs appear. A professional service should cover the same three jobs.
bullets: A mouse can fit through a hole the width of a pencil, 1/4 inch (6 mm) across, according to the CDC.
The University of Nebraska's rough guide for a new infestation in a 1,500-square-foot structure is two dozen properly placed snap traps, spaced no more than about 10 feet apart where mice are active.
The CDC says to air out a room or outbuilding for 30 minutes, and a vehicle for 20 minutes, before cleaning up after mice.
The CDC's bleach solution is 1.5 cups of household bleach in 1 gallon of water, left to soak on droppings and nests for 5 minutes.
Cornell University says a mouse that dies inside a wall produces a smell that can last for days, compared with weeks for a rat.
The CDC says to contact a professional rodent exterminating service when there is evidence of rodents in heating and cooling ducts.

body.text: What does mice removal involve?

Mice removal is three jobs done in order: close the holes the mice use, trap the ones already inside, and clean up what they left behind. [The University of Nebraska-Lincoln's house mouse guide](https://extensionpubs.unl.edu/publication/g1105/html/view) sums up effective control as sanitation, exclusion and population reduction, and the [University of California's house mouse guide](https://ipm.ucanr.edu/home-and-landscape/house-mouse/) (UC IPM) says that when dealing with an infestation, some form of population reduction is almost always necessary. The [complete guide to mouse control](/learn/mice) covers biology, signs and prevention in full. This page concentrates on getting mice out of particular parts of a home and cleaning up afterward.
Seal the entry holes first

Sealing comes first. The [CDC's trapping page](https://www.cdc.gov/healthy-pets/rodent-control/trap-up.html) tells readers who see evidence of rodents to first check inside and outside the home for how they got in and to seal those holes, and then to set traps for any rodents that may still be inside. The [CDC's seal-up instructions](https://www.cdc.gov/healthy-pets/rodent-control/seal-up.html) say a mouse can fit through a hole the width of a pencil, 1/4 inch (6 mm) across, and UC IPM adds that mice squeeze under gaps 1/4 inch tall and through openings 3/8 inch wide. The CDC's fix for small holes is steel wool held in place with caulk or spray foam. For larger holes it lists lath screen or metal, cement, hardware cloth and metal sheeting.

The sources differ on foam and on how long steel wool lasts. UC IPM lists expanding foam with plastic screening, rubber, vinyl and wood as gnawable materials that are ineffective for plugging holes, calls steel wool a good temporary plug that may rust over time, and says to seal foundation cracks and the openings around pipes, vents and utility cables with metal or concrete.

Nebraska's guide uses sealant or mortar for gaps of less than 1/2 inch around pipes, copper woven-wire mesh or stainless steel fibers (neither of which rusts) packed into larger gaps and finished with sealant or mortar, and wood, aluminum flashing, concrete or 1/4-inch wire mesh over larger openings. Read together, they point to metal, concrete or mortar as the barrier, with foam only holding the metal in place. The steps are laid out in [how to pack a mouse hole with steel wool and caulk](/blog/steel-wool-for-mice).
Trap the mice already inside

Use snap traps, and use more of them than seems necessary. The CDC's trapping instructions call for traditional snap traps with a small amount of chunky peanut butter on the bait pan, set with the baited end next to the wall so the trap and the wall form a T. UC IPM says to space traps no more than about 10 feet apart where mice are active and notes that pairs set 1 to 2 inches apart can increase the catch. Nebraska's guide gives two dozen properly placed snap traps as a rough guide for a new infestation in a 1,500-square-foot structure, and it says to check traps in the morning because mice are most active before dawn and after dusk.

The sources split on glue boards and live traps. UC IPM and Nebraska both describe glue boards as an alternative to traps and multiple-capture traps as a way to catch several mice without resetting, but each adds cautions: UC IPM says adult rodents can often detect and avoid the glue and that mice caught alive have to be euthanized, and Nebraska does not recommend live-catch box traps because mice should not be relocated. [Cornell University's rodent management guide](https://cals.cornell.edu/integrated-pest-management/outreach-education/whats-bugging-you/rodents/managing-mice-and-rats) calls glue traps not ideal for rodent management. The CDC says not to use glue traps or live traps, because they can scare a rodent into urinating, which can increase your chance of getting sick.

Releasing a live mouse has a legal side as well: UC IPM notes that in California it is illegal to relocate live wildlife, house mice included, away from the property where it was captured without a special state permit. The guide to [mouse trap types and placement](/blog/mice-traps) compares the designs, and a separate page looks at [what humane mouse control means in practice](/blog/how-to-get-rid-of-mice-humanely).
Know when the mice are gone

The CDC's test is a week with no rodents captured and no new signs of them. While the traps are out, it says to check them daily and dispose of any dead rodents immediately, to check the bait every week, refilling or moving it as needed, for at least 15 days, and to leave baited traps out longer if mice are still present. Small messes can be cleaned as you find them, using [the CDC's cleanup method](https://www.cdc.gov/healthy-pets/rodent-control/clean-up.html) described further down. It makes sense to leave the full cleanout of an attic, crawl space or garage until the clear week has passed, so you are not disinfecting a space that mice are still using.
How do you get mice out of walls, attics, crawl spaces and garages?

Trap and seal in every one of these spaces; the method does not change from one part of the house to another, only where the traps go and which openings need closing. The CDC names attics, basements and crawl spaces, along with other areas without regular human traffic, as places to put traps, and it tells homeowners to seal outbuildings and garages as well as the house.

body.text: Mice in the walls

You do not have to open a wall to remove the mice living in it; trap them where they come out. For mice in wall spaces, Nebraska's guide directs attention to the places they exit, such as along pipes, above drop ceilings and on foundation sill plates. It gives that advice for bait stations, but the same exit points are where a trap will be crossed. The CDC's indoor trap sites fit the pattern: behind the stove and refrigerator and in the back of cabinets and drawers. Its seal-up list names the matching holes, including the gaps around pipes under sinks and washing machines and around pipes to water heaters and furnaces.

Poison bait is a poor fit for wall voids. Cornell's guide explains that feeding on bait does not send rodents outdoors in search of water; they tire and look for a protected place. UC IPM says rodenticide use will often result in house mice dying inside the structure and that trapping may be the best approach where that is a problem. The guide to [mouse poison and its risks](/blog/mice-poison) covers the active ingredients and the hazards to pets and wildlife.
Mice in the attic

Trap along the edges of the attic and beside any droppings, then close the roofline gaps that let the mice in. Mice reach attics because, as Nebraska's guide describes, they can climb any rough vertical surface and balance along horizontal wire cables or ropes; a separate page explains [how mice climb walls and reach upper floors](/blog/can-mice-climb-walls). On the outside, the CDC says to check the roof among the rafters, gables, eaves and soffits, and around attic vents.

Attic cleanup has two extra rules from the CDC. Exposed insulation contaminated with urine and droppings goes into plastic bags for removal. Storage boxes and containers that may be contaminated should be moved outside to a well-ventilated area in direct sunlight, and the CDC says to stay upwind while emptying them so dust and debris do not blow toward your face. Cardboard boxes soiled with urine or droppings are thrown out, while plastic, glass and metal containers can be disinfected.
Mice in a crawl space or basement

Set traps along the foundation walls and sill plates, and seal from the outside. The CDC's outdoor checklist includes the gap between the foundation and the ground, the area around crawl space vents, and the holes for electrical, plumbing, cable and gas lines. It also advises using flashing around the base of the house and fixing gaps in trailer skirting. Of the materials Nebraska's guide lists for larger openings, 1/4-inch wire mesh is the one that still lets a vent pass air.

For cleanup, the CDC's instruction for the dirt floors of outbuildings is to spray them with disinfectant, where a hard floor would be mopped. The CDC's seal-up page adds that you can contact a pest control specialist if rodents have gotten into areas that cannot be reached to clean, a description that fits a crawl space too tight to work in.
Mice in the garage

Start with the doors. UC IPM's figure is that mice squeeze under gaps 1/4 inch tall, and it says doors, windows and screens should fit tightly, with metal over the edges where gnawing is a problem. One page covers [sealing the corner gaps of a garage door](/blog/mouse-proof-garage-door-seal-canada) in detail. Inside, Nebraska's guide says to keep food, pet food included, in tight-fitting bins and, whenever possible, to store materials at least 8 inches off the ground and at least 1 foot away from walls. UC IPM suggests searching behind boxes, in drawers and around woodpiles for nests of finely shredded paper or other fibrous material.
How do you get mice out of a car or truck?

Trap around the parked vehicle, then air it out and disinfect it before you drive it or vacuum it. The CDC advises placing traps in outbuildings and in areas likely to serve as rodent shelters, a description that fits the garage or carport where a vehicle sits, and it notes that rodents may nest in cars, trucks and campers, especially ones that are used infrequently. For the vehicle itself, the CDC's instructions run in this order, with the vehicle in a well-ventilated space:

items: Open the hood, the doors and the trunk, and let the interior and the engine compartment air out for 20 minutes.
Inspect the air intakes and filters before starting the engine, and check the interior.
Remove the cables from the battery before inspecting the engine compartment, to avoid a shock. Wear plastic gloves and a long-sleeved shirt.
Find any dead rodents, nesting material, droppings or urine.
Do not use a vacuum or a high-pressure sprayer on droppings, urine or contaminated surfaces until they have been disinfected.
Spray the material with disinfectant until fully soaked, let it sit for 5 minutes or as the label directs, then pick it up with a paper towel and put it in the garbage.
Clean the rest of the area with more disinfectant, and reconnect the battery once the area is dry.
Wash your gloved hands with soap and water or disinfectant before taking the gloves off, then wash your bare hands with soap and warm water.

body.text: If there is nesting material in the air intake system, the CDC says to remove both the nesting material and the air filter and to fit a new replacement filter. It also suggests consulting a qualified mechanic or automotive professional for assistance. A clean vehicle that goes back to the same parking spot can be nested in again, so finish by trapping and sealing the building it is kept in. A separate guide covers [how to keep mice out of a parked car's engine bay and cabin](/blog/how-to-keep-mice-out-of-your-car).
How do you find and remove a dead mouse, and how long does the smell last?

Check every trap and bait placement, work toward where the odor is strongest, and remove the carcass with gloves, disinfectant and two sealed bags; by Cornell's account the smell of a mouse left inside a wall can last for days. A dead mouse you cannot see is a known side effect of poison bait. Nebraska's guide says it is impossible to predict where a poisoned mouse will die, and it dismisses the idea that poisoned mice head outside for water as hopeful speculation.

items: **Start with what you set.** Check each trap, including any pushed behind an appliance or left in the attic or garage.
**Go where mice travel.** Look behind the stove and refrigerator, in the back of cabinets and drawers, and where pipes enter the wall, the places the CDC lists for traps and for entry holes.
**Check low and high.** Cornell's inspection advice covers both under furniture and inside drop ceilings.
**Narrow it down.** Compare rooms, then cabinets, then sections of wall, moving toward the strongest odor.

body.text: How do you remove the carcass?

Put on rubber or plastic gloves, spray the mouse and the area around it with bleach solution or disinfectant, and let it soak for 5 minutes or as the disinfectant label directs. The CDC then says to place the mouse in a plastic bag, along with the trap if you are discarding it, knot the bag, put it inside a second bag, knot that one, and put it in a covered garbage can that is emptied regularly. Because fleas are common on rodents, the CDC also suggests considering an EPA-registered insect repellent on clothing, shoes and hands, used as its label directs, while picking up dead rodents and nesting material.

Nebraska's guide describes a tidy way to do the pickup: turn a sealable plastic bag inside out over your hand, grasp the mouse, pull the bag right side out around it and seal it. To reuse a snap trap, the CDC says to submerge the trap and the mouse in a bucket of disinfectant for 5 minutes, lift the metal bar to drop the mouse into a plastic bag, then rinse the trap well with water and let it dry completely.
How long does a dead mouse smell?

Days for a mouse, by Cornell's account, compared with weeks for a rat. Cornell does not give a tighter figure, and Nebraska's guide lists the variables: whether dead mice cause an odor at all depends on how many died, where they died, the relative humidity and airflow, the size of the mice and how sensitive the resident's nose is.

Removal is still worth the effort when the carcass can be reached. Cornell notes that dead rodents left in place can attract carpet beetles and clothes moths, which feed on the hair and skin of the carcass and eventually on wool rugs and clothing. None of the sources used for this page evaluates odor absorbers or deodorizing sprays; the only remedy they describe is removing the carcass. For a single mouse inside a finished wall, weigh Cornell's time frame of days against the cost of opening and repairing the wall.
How do you clean up mouse droppings and nests safely?

Wet the droppings with disinfectant before you touch them, and never sweep or vacuum them. That is the core of the CDC's method, and Nebraska's guide gives the same instruction: no household vacuum or broom, only a wet towel, rag or mop. If you are not sure what you are looking at, see [what mouse droppings look like and how to tell fresh from old](/blog/what-does-mouse-poop-look-like-canada). The CDC's steps for a room, shed or other outbuilding are:

items: Open all doors and windows for 30 minutes before cleaning, and leave the area while it airs out.
Put on rubber or plastic gloves.

Mix a fresh bleach solution of 1.5 cups of household bleach in 1 gallon of water (1 part bleach to 9 parts water), or use a general-purpose household cleaner that has the word disinfectant on its label, according to that label.
Spray the urine, droppings and nesting material until very wet, and let them soak for 5 minutes or for the time on the disinfectant label.
Wipe up the material with paper towels and put it in a covered garbage can that is emptied regularly. Nests and dead mice go into a plastic bag that is knotted and placed inside a second knotted bag.
Mop hard floors, and clean countertops, cabinets and drawers with disinfectant.
Wash your gloved hands with soap and water or disinfectant before taking the gloves off, then wash your bare hands with soap and warm water.

body.title: No broom, no vacuum
body.text: The CDC says not to sweep or vacuum rodent urine, droppings or nesting material, because doing so can send tiny droplets containing viruses into the air. Nebraska's guide calls it critical that the droppings and the dust around them do not become airborne.

body.text: How do you clean fabrics, carpets, papers and insulation?
Launder what can be washed hot, shampoo or steam clean rugs and upholstery, give papers sunlight or time, and bag soiled insulation for removal. The CDC's instruction for each material:

body.text: When is a cleanup too big to handle yourself?

When the infestation is heavy or the mice have reached the ductwork. The CDC says special precautions should be used when cleaning homes or buildings with a heavy rodent infestation, and its equipment list for people doing that work goes well past gloves: coveralls (disposable if possible), rubber boots or disposable shoe covers, protective goggles, and a half-mask air-purifying respirator with a high efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filter or a powered air-purifying respirator with HEPA filters. Nebraska's guide likewise calls for additional protective measures where fecal contamination is substantial or spread over a large area, or where deer mice or white-footed mice have been identified.

For ducts, the CDC is direct: contact a professional rodent exterminating service to remove rodents when there is evidence that they have gotten into heating and cooling ventilation systems. It adds that companies specializing in duct cleaning are familiar with the problems and risks of rodent infestation in ventilation systems. It also suggests contacting your local health department with questions about your specific situation.
Can you get sick from removing mice or cleaning up after them?

It is possible, which is why the CDC's method keeps droppings wet and your hands gloved. UC IPM lists leptospirosis, salmonella and lymphocytic choriomeningitis (LCM) among the diseases house mice carry. It says LCM is contracted through exposure to fresh urine, droppings, saliva or nesting materials from infected house mice, and it gives an estimate, without naming its source, that 5 percent of house mice across the United States carry the virus and are able to transmit it. It also notes that exposure to proteins in house mouse urine has been linked to early onset of asthma in sensitive children.

Hantavirus is a separate question. Nebraska's guide states that house mice are not known to be carriers of hantavirus. The same guide names deer mice and white-footed mice (*Peromyscus* species) as known carriers and, because few people can identify the rodents in their home, advises caution during all cleanup. If the mice you caught might be deer mice, read [how to recognize deer mice and why they call for extra care](/blog/deer-mice), and compare your catch against [the types of mice found in US homes](/blog/types-of-mice) before a large cleanup.
The CDC's advice on illness is short: talk to a healthcare provider if you think a recent illness may be due to a rodent-borne disease, and tell them about any exposure to rodents.
What does a professional mice removal service include?

A complete professional job should cover the same ground the extension guides lay out for anyone: an inspection, trapping, exclusion and sanitation. Service names vary from company to company, so compare what each quote covers, not what the service is called.

How many visits are included and who checks the traps between them

Which holes will be sealed and with what materials

Removing droppings, nests and soiled insulation, and disinfecting surfaces

body.text: A professional also has access to products the public does not. Nebraska's guide notes that pest management professionals can use restricted use pesticides registered for mice, for the rare occasions when general-use rodenticides cannot resolve a problem. For a heavy cleanup, ask whether the crew uses the coveralls and respirators on the CDC's list. Prices, timelines and the license check are covered in the guide to [hiring a mice exterminator](/blog/mice-exterminator).
Should you remove mice yourself or hire a professional?

Do it yourself when the signs are limited to places you can reach and you are able to seal the holes. Hire it out when trapping has stalled, the mice are in the ductwork, or the contamination is heavy or out of reach.

body.text: If you take the do-it-yourself route, the [guides to rodent traps, stations and exclusion materials](/pest-product-guides/rodent-control) explain the product types, and a broader page sets out [when do-it-yourself pest control makes sense](/blog/diy-pest-control). Whichever way you go, the job is finished only when the holes are closed, a week has passed with empty traps and no new signs, and the droppings are gone.

howTo.name: How to remove mice from a house and clean up after them

steps.name: Find the activity
steps.text: Look for droppings, gnaw marks, footprints and oily brown rub marks, checking low under furniture and appliances and high inside drop ceilings.

steps.name: Seal the entry holes
steps.text: Close every opening a quarter inch or larger using steel wool held in place with caulk, hardware cloth, metal sheeting or cement.

steps.name: Set snap traps
steps.text: Bait snap traps with a small amount of chunky peanut butter and place them with the baited end against the wall, no more than about 10 feet apart.

steps.name: Empty the traps
steps.text: Check traps daily. Wearing gloves, spray each dead mouse with disinfectant, wait five minutes, seal it inside two knotted plastic bags and put it in a covered garbage can.

steps.name: Keep trapping until a week is clear
steps.text: Check the bait weekly for at least 15 days, refilling or moving it as needed, and continue until a full week passes with no captures and no new signs of mice.

steps.name: Air out the space
steps.text: Open all doors and windows for 30 minutes before cleaning and stay out of the area while it ventilates.

steps.name: Soak droppings and nests
steps.text: Spray urine, droppings and nesting material with bleach solution or disinfectant until very wet and let them soak for five minutes. Do not sweep or vacuum.

steps.name: Wipe up and disinfect
steps.text: Wipe up the soaked material with paper towels, put it in a covered garbage can, then mop hard floors and clean hard surfaces with disinfectant.

steps.name: Wash up
steps.text: Wash your gloved hands with soap and water or disinfectant, remove the gloves, then wash your hands with soap and warm water.

faqs.question: How long does it take to get rid of mice in a house?
faqs.answer: No source gives a single figure, but the CDC's instructions point to a couple of weeks at the least. It says to check traps daily, to check the bait every week and refill or move it as needed for at least 15 days, and to leave baited traps out longer if mice are still present. It treats the rodents as gone when a full week passes with none captured and no new signs. The University of California advises using enough traps to make the trapping period short and decisive, spaced no more than about 10 feet apart where mice are active. Sealing the entry holes at the start keeps new mice from restarting the count.

faqs.question: Will mice leave on their own if the food is removed?
faqs.answer: Not reliably. The University of Nebraska says total elimination of mice through sanitation alone is almost impossible, because mice can survive in small areas with limited food and shelter and no water. Waiting also gives them time to multiply: the University of California says a female house mouse may have 5 to 10 litters of about 5 or 6 pups each in a single year. Storing food in tight-fitting containers and clearing clutter still helps by taking away food and cover, but it has to be combined with sealing and trapping.

faqs.question: Can you vacuum mouse droppings?
faqs.answer: No. The CDC says not to vacuum or sweep rodent urine, droppings or nesting material, because that can send tiny droplets containing viruses into the air, and the University of Nebraska says not to use a household vacuum or broom to collect droppings. Spray them with a bleach solution of 1.5 cups of household bleach per gallon of water, or a disinfectant used as its label directs, let them soak for 5 minutes, and wipe them up with paper towels. In its instructions for vehicles, the CDC says not to use a vacuum on contaminated surfaces until they have been disinfected. If you have already vacuumed, the CDC says to follow its cleanup guidance.

faqs.question: What should you wear to clean up after mice?
faqs.answer: For an ordinary cleanup, the CDC calls for rubber or plastic gloves, washed while still on your hands before you take them off. For a heavy infestation it lists more: coveralls, disposable if possible, rubber boots or disposable shoe covers, protective goggles, and a half-mask air-purifying respirator with a HEPA filter or a powered air-purifying respirator with HEPA filters. The University of Nebraska also advises additional protective measures where droppings are substantial or spread over a large area. If your cleanup looks like the second kind, the CDC suggests contacting your local health department with questions about your situation, and hiring the work out is a reasonable alternative.

faqs.question: Is it better to use poison or traps to remove mice?
faqs.answer: Traps, in most homes. The University of Nebraska lists four advantages of trapping: it is pesticide free, it shows its results, it works in many locations, and it lets you dispose of the mice before they cause an odor. The CDC recommends traditional snap traps, says to use poison or bait stations only for infestations that persist, and recommends EPA-registered products. Cornell University notes that feeding on bait does not make rodents leave the house in search of water; they look for a protected place, and a mouse that dies inside a wall can smell for days. Any rodenticide must be used exactly as its label directs.
